@BEP
This concerns your map of the top of the castle.
RPG Maker has an implied perspective of semi-looking down.  You therefore need to create the illusion that you are sort of looking over the top of the wall.  You can do that by 2 simple things.
First you use shift+click mapping to make it look like your carpets are continuing down to meet the wall.
Secondly, you place the pillars in such a way as to make it look like the bottom section is also behind the wall.
I've done a very fast mock-up for you to show what I mean.  I do not have your tile set, so I've just used some wall or other and a red carpet.  None of my interior tile sets have pillars, so imagine that the cupboards are pillars.  I used the snip tool for speed, rather than taking a proper screen shot, so sorry if it's a bit blurred.
Spoiler:
example of looking over the top of the wall
I hope that shows clearly enough what the difference is.  If your walls are high, then you would show even less of the pillar in order to make the map look consistent and have the stairs finish one tile lower than you do.

posts.author: Kes
posts.body:
@Scorpioni
An interesting map.  It looks like the sort of place it would be nice for the player to visit.  I do have some queries, though.
Your inn and the house next to it are both mapped so that the implied back wall is literally at the water's edge.  No building would be like that, there would be at least one tile between the building and the water.
That house also has a vine growing from the lower roof up past the bedroom window.  What is it growing from?  There is no soil, or pot or whatever for its roots.
The house in the northwest corner - the little ground floor extension would not only be casting a shadow on the ground, it would also be casting it on the lower part of the main section as well.  Without it the perspective is lost.  I suggest you consider making a shadow graphic on one of your tilesets and applying it with an event so that it doesn't mess up your window graphic.
Finally the coach (nice graphic, btw) is a bit of a puzzle.  It cannot have got there from the south, as the entrance is up steep steps.  If it came from the north, how did it get across the bridge and negotiate its way past the first stall?  Maybe you need to make your bridge one tile wider on the east side?

posts.author: MarxMayhem
posts.body:
Behold! The entrance to my debug room!
One thing y'all may notice is the perspective. By using the UltraMode7 plugin, I adjusted the viewpoint very slightly so that the map is no longer a rectangle but an isosceles trapezoid. Because the view of the map is distorted, actors and events appear popped out and invokes a sense of 3D. When you "feel" that the things in the world can pop out, you add some soul into it.
This has one weakness, and that anything that isn't an actor or event will also appear as flat with the map- you can notice this with the pillars. The answer to this is simple and applied to the buildings: Make buildings out of events. This way, they too will pop out, and the more things that pop out at a time, the more alive it feels.
There are things that this method has to address to be effective, but my art focus is in making character and effects assets at this time, so I'll consider this an opportunity to receive feedback.

posts.author: Kes
posts.body:
@mmKALLL
I'll just comment about the first map, as that has a number of issues common to the others.
You seem to have mixed up the different terrains in a not very logical way.  If the ground is soft enough and rich enough to have those strong earthy patches, it is unlikely
also
to have patches which look sandy.  Given the general lushness, the sandy (desert?) patches look out of place.  I would stick to earth patches.  Your cliffs are brown, but suddenly there's a patch of grey rock under the camp fire.  As a general rule, try not to mix lots of different terrains in a smallish area unless you have a
very
good reason for it.
That lower bridge has no logic to it at all.  It looks as if you have to walk over your crops to get from one side to the other.  Why would anyone plant crops like that?  You can't weed them without either running to the upper bridge, cross over, run down again to get the crops on the other side - still leaving you to walk over them to get to the crops in the middle.  Maps cannot be ultra realistic, but they do have to have a reasonable degree of plausibility.  I'd put the crops somewhere else.  A useful thing to do with all maps is to ask yourself : " Why is it like this?"  Maps tell a story without words, so what story do I want it to tell the player and what story is it actually telling?
Your hills are not that high, (scarcely taller than your tent) so it is unlikely that you are going to move straight to desert, complete with dried up grass and cacti.  This is especially the case where you have a broad river gushing down - that would naturally irrigate the ground.  I'd have the tops mostly grass.
It is, I think, very difficult to mix autotile trees and more naturalistic trees and shrubs on the same map.
You have a broad river moving at some speed as it comes down from the hills,  which suddenly narrows to a single tile width and is shallow enough to have what look like stepping stones to get across.  This fails the plausibility test.
What the map lacks is coherence.  It feels like a lot of elements have been jumbled together in order to give it "variety".  Things don't seem like they fit together in any obvious way.
Don't be discouraged if you haven't yet got the feel of how a map should go.  This only comes with a lot of practice, and studying how other people do things.  Try and work out specifically why something looks good, not just why something doesn't work.

I don't know which tileset you are using, but the default MV tiles have a dirt path.  This would, imo, be much better than the white tile you are using.  No map can be ultra realistic, but try to have something that looks in keeping with the general terrain you want to show. I'm fairly sure that MV's default tiles have a better swamp tile than the one you are using.  Although still fairly boxy, it is nothing like as much as the tile you have used.
Another variation - if you want something simplified as a style, and this map is just a way of getting the player from one point to another, try using the World Map tile set. Been working on a survival dungeon crawler as a side project. So far I have:
1.) Survival stats linked to the hud. Stats give detriments when reached. For example at 35% rest you will lose strength stats, and max hp. At 0% you will lose 1/2 of both. For hunger and thirst when you reach 0% you will lose health until you die.
2.)Working lantern that uses oil, and usage is linked to the hud. If it runs out of oil the lamp turns off. You can refill it with oil flasks, which give you back an empty bottle when used.
3.) If you die, you drop your souls on the ground, and a physical soul is represented where you died in the game world. If you die before picking up these souls, they will disappear and you will drop your current souls at your most current location of death. (Yes this is a direct ripoff of dark souls, I love the mechanic.)
4.)Node based world map travel
5.)Weight system. Everything has weight, and if you are overburdened you cannot hold any more. Also adds infinite storage to your house.

posts.author: Kes

@Former_Sky
Just a couple of suggestions to tidy things up a bit.
In the campfire scene, I'd have the sprites closer to the fire, otherwise it looks like they've had an argument - though perhaps they have, in which case leave them where they are. It might also help to have some indication of belongings e.g. a sack which could pass as a back pack, a sleeping mat, just something to give a hint that this is a real stopping point.
When I'm planning what houses look like on the exterior, I always try and imagine what the interior would have to be like for that to work.  Using that criterion, have a look at the chimney on the house on the right.  It would of necessity have to be above the fire place, but that fireplace would have to be right next to the front door.  This helps explain why it looks odd where it is.  I'd move it up to the top of the roof.  As a general rule anyway, chimneys rarely come out of the middle of the roof, they come out at the top.
@cddeat03
I think you need to edit the cliff faces as well, because having them the same brightness for both day and night doesn't work, imo.
As for the corn and earth patches, I don't think just making them darker (which in the case of the earth patch on the right actually makes it stand out more clearly) is the best method.  Perhaps try some desaturation and reduced brightness?

VXAce tiles are 32 x 32 instead of 48x48.  Therefore an Ace 3-high cliff face, for example, will automatically be smaller.  Place those cliffs on the map at some distance from an MV/MZ cliff, making sure top and bottom are equi-distant relative to the larger cliff, and you have the illusion of perspective, making it seem that the Ace cliff is further away. posts.author: Kes

@Descendancy
You're going to probably hate my opening remark, but I think if you're just starting out on parallaxing you might benefit from hearing it.  And it's this.  If you hadn't told me that map was a parallax I would have assumed it was just made in the editor.  It seems to me that parallaxes should be used when you want to do something the editor cannot do, otherwise the massive amount of extra time needed, as well as the far bigger file size it produces, doesn't make it worth while.  I would like to suggest that before doing another parallax map you clearly identify what the 'extra' will be that the parallax is going to bring.
You also said that this was your first serious map in general.  I would strongly urge you to learn how to map in the editor first so that you can quickly and easily change things around dramatically.  It's far quicker to move a house in the editor than in a parallax.
Just treating this map as a map and disregarding how it was done - I would concentrate first on getting your roofs right.  Take this one, for example
I think what you are trying to convey is the idea that the house extends further forward on the left side than on the right.  However, the way those tiles work the more you have, the higher the top of the roof.  They do not extend backwards, only upwards.  So you have a house with a height of what looks like 7 tiles on the left but magically it only has a height of 5 on the right.  If you want a house which extends like that you will have to use a different form of tile.  Maybe something like this.  This is a simple farm house, done in the editor (as are all of my maps) which extends forward.  If you could up the number of tiles of both parts you will find that the total from ridge to ground is the same.
I chose this one for a second reason.  Notice the way the ridges of the 2 parts are in alignment and the edge of the roof (where the rainwater gutter would be on a modern house) also line up.  Now compare it with your house where you have that sort of arrangement.
Your gutter line runs up the roof of the left hand section and then the end of the roof sticks up out into the air.  You will not find a roof like that anywhere in the world.  It would be virtually impossible to build, because for the back end of the roof to be that far off the ground, the whole side of the house would have to be built on a slant with the back wall considerably higher than the front wall.
